item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: Wisdom, mythology, and the prefrontal cortex: a neurocognitive interpretation of Athena's birth.
item.description:
Postgraduate medical journal
BACKGROUND: The myth of Athena's birth from Zeus' forehead presents a symbolic narrative that resonates with modern neuroscientific perspectives. The prefrontal cortex, crucial for decision-making, foresight, and moral reasoning, aligns intriguingly with the ancient attribution of wisdom to the head. This study aims to explore the convergence of mythology, philosophy, visual art, and neuroscience in order to examine whether ancient cultural narratives implicitly localized wisdom in the brain. METHODS: A multidisciplinary approach was employed, drawing on classical texts, iconographic traditions, and contemporary neurobiological models of wisdom.Comparative analysis was used to identify symbolic parallels between mythological representations and neurocognitive functions. RESULTS: The cranial emergence of Athena can be interpreted as a cultural archetype that anticipates the modern understanding of higher-order cognition. Artistic depictions reinforce this correspondence by emphasizing the head as the seat of wisdom. Despite the risk of anachronism, the recurrence of this imagery across centuries suggests that myth may encode latent insights into brain function. CONCLUSIONS: The case of Athena's birth highlights how mythological narratives can serve as proto-scientific frameworks for understanding human cognition. Integrating insights from mythology and neuroscience may enrich both historical interpretation and contemporary discussions on the nature of wisdom.

item.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in the Executive Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks. Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187). Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use. Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

item.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

item.title: Inter-subject functional variability of gray and white matter during methadone maintenance treatment and its association with gene expression profiles.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Methadone maintenance treatment(MMT) for opioid use disorder(OUD) may cause changes in brain functional heterogeneity whose molecular mechanisms remain unknown. This study aims to investigate MMT-related gray/white matter inter-subject variability functional connectivity(GM/WM-IVFC) alterations and to associate them with clinical and transcriptomic characteristics. Between March 2017 and June 2026, a total of 244 participants were voluntarily enrolled from detoxification centers, drug rehabilitation clinics, and society in Hunan Province, China, including MMT group(N = 44), individuals with sustained heroin self-abstinence and no lifetime MMT(HSA, N = 42), short-term abstinent heroin users at baseline(OUD1, N = 62) and 10-month opioid-free follow-up(OUD2, N = 43), and two healthy control cohorts(HC1, N = 48; HC2, N = 48) respectively age/gender-matched with MMT/HSA groups and OUD1. OUD1/2 and HSA groups were used to exploratively investigate the influence of previous heroin use and non-MMT abstinence duration on IVFC. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) data were acquired and analyzed to extract GM/WM-IVFC metrics, which were compared ROI-wise between groups and correlated with neuropsychological scales. Transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas(AHBA) were integrated via partial least squares(PLS) regression and functional enrichment analyses to further identify gene expression profiles underlying IVFC alterations. After Bonferroni correction, compared to HC1, MMT group exhibited the most widespread IVFC increases, spanning 20 GM and 7 WM regions. HSA group shared some overlapping GM-IVFC elevations with MMT group in bilateral orbital parts of inferior frontal gyrus and thalamus, yet its overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions was lower than that of MMT group. Neither OUD1 nor OUD2 showed difference in overall mean IVFC of significant GM regions from HC2. Both OUD1/2 displayed elevated overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions relative to HC2. Then, the overall mean IVFC of significant GM/WM regions between MMT group and HC1 were positively correlated with impulsivity, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and daily methadone dose. PLS regression linked IVFC patterns to AHBA transcriptomic profiles in MMT group, with enriched pathways in neuroinflammation, synaptic function, glutamatergic signaling, and neuronal development. These findings indicate that MMT is accompanied by cerebral IVFC elevations, whose linkages with neuropsychological aberrations and gene profiles implicate IVFC as a latent clinical phenotype for managing MMT-related complications.

item.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

item.title: Association of scan time with resting-state functional connectivity discriminability: effects of temporal alignment.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is increasingly used to probe individual differences in brain organization, but individual-level FC discriminability may vary across repeated acquisitions related to arousal, physiology, and endogenous brain state. Acquisition-time variation may be a systematic contributor to this variability, yet its impact on FC discriminability has not been well characterized. Multi-session resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project were analyzed using minimally preprocessed and ICA-FIX-denoised BOLD time series. Whole-brain and network-level FC matrices were constructed after atlas-based parcellation, and sessions were grouped into one-hour daytime bins. Discriminability was computed to quantify how well repeated FC profiles from the same individual could be distinguished from those of other individuals, and grouped versus ungrouped estimates were compared. Temporal alignment of scans according to acquisition time substantially improved FC discriminability across both test-retest configurations. Whole-brain discriminability increased from 0.29 to 0.61 in one configuration and from 0.31 to 0.60 in the other. Similar gains were observed across canonical networks, with robust improvements in the default mode, dorsal attention, frontoparietal, and visual networks. These findings show that acquisition-time grouping was associated with higher FC discriminability in this HCP sample. Incorporating acquisition-time structure into rs-fMRI acquisition and analysis may enhance connectome fingerprinting and improve FC discriminability.

item.title: Complex Spatial and Temporal Organization of Functional Brain Networks
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent research exploring brain-behavior associations has relied on the language of complex systems to understand how stable behavioral individual differences emerge from brain function. At the same time, advances in neuroimaging have provided greater insight into both the topological and temporal properties of macroscale cortical networks. These new approaches offer a potential avenue for understanding how functional activity in the brain might behave in a manner that aligns with complex-systems interpretations of psychological traits. The present study used resting-state data from the Human Connectome project (N = 994) to explore associations between the spatial and temporal features of functional brain networks. Using an adaptive frequency approach to explore brain function at different timescales together with a family of methods from complex systems theory, we identified patterns of brain state organization reflecting a state-trait continuum, with more stable trait-like dynamics and greater functional coupling between networks in lower frequency oscillations. Additionally, we found evidence of greater coupling across timescales in brain networks associated with higher-order cognition. This research supports interpretations of brain organization as a spatiotemporal hierarchy and provides future avenues for exploring brain-behavior associations from a complex system perspective.

item.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.

item.title: Multidimensional Neural Maturity Indices from Naturalistic fMRI Reveal the Longitudinal Development of Theory of Mind.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Theory of Mind (ToM) develops from early reasoning about others' beliefs and intentions toward more advanced forms of recursive and socially embedded mental-state understanding. This ability emerges alongside the progressive maturation of large-scale brain networks. Here, we introduce a multidimensional neural maturity framework, derived from naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), that characterizes children's neurofunctional maturation along three dimensions: functional connectivity, temporal fluctuation, and spatial activation, by capturing neural responses to social narratives. Using an accelerated longitudinal design (baseline ages 3-9 years; 27-30-month follow-up), we applied this framework to examine how social-cognitive brain networks mature across complementary dimensions of brain function and how such maturation relates to ToM development. Across childhood, all three neural indices increased longitudinally, indicating progressive maturation of social-cognitive networks. Brain-behavior analyses further highlighted temporal fluctuation and spatial activation maturity as dimensions most closely related to ToM performance. Longitudinal path models indicated developmental continuity from elementary to advanced ToM, and suggested that advanced mental-state reasoning develops in coordination with the multidimensional longitudinal maturation of social-cognitive neural responses. Together, these findings provide initial longitudinal neurodevelopmental evidence that children's social-cognitive networks become increasingly adult-like across multiple neurofunctional dimension, offering a neurodevelopmental extension of behavioral accounts of the transition from elementary to advanced mental-state reasoning.

item.title: EEG Microstate Alterations and Their Association with Cognitive Performance in Late-Onset Epilepsy of Unknown Etiology: Comparison with Alzheimer's Disease.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
Background Cognitive impairment is common in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU), but its electrophysiological correlates and relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. We compared resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate dynamics among LOEU, AD, and cognitively normal (CN) groups and examined their associations with cognitive performance. Methods Eyes-closed 32-channel resting-state EEG recordings were analyzed from 60 patients with LOEU, 65 with AD, and 60 CN participants. Four canonical microstate classes (A-D) were identified. Group differences in microstate parameters were tested with false discovery rate correction. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores were examined using multivariable interaction models adjusted for age, sex, education, and cerebral small vessel disease burden. Results Microstate B duration was longer in LOEU and AD than in CN (Holm-adjusted p=0.011 and 0.016), whereas microstate C occurrence was lower in both patient groups (p=0.001 and 0.018). Microstate D duration was longer in LOEU than in CN and AD (both p=0.038). For microstate A duration, the group interaction survived false discovery rate correction for MMSE (q=0.0255) but not MoCA (q=0.122). In LOEU, longer microstate A duration was associated with lower MoCA and MMSE scores. Pairwise slope comparisons were more negative in LOEU than in CN for both outcomes, whereas LOEU-AD slope differences were not significant. Conclusions LOEU showed altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics that partly overlapped with those observed in AD, alongside a group difference in microstate D duration. Microstate A duration was associated with cognitive performance in LOEU, although this association did not significantly differ from that observed in AD. These findings support further investigation of EEG microstates as electrophysiological correlates of cognitive dysfunction in LOEU while also highlighting overlap with AD.

item.title: Altered directional brain-heart interactions across resting states and frequency bands in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Background Schizophrenia is associated with abnormalities in cortical activity and autonomic regulation, but directional brain-heart interaction (BHI) across resting states and frequency bands remains unclear. Methods Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG) were recorded simultaneously in 33 medicated men with schizophrenia and 29 healthy men during eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Directional BHI was assessed across two coupling directions, two cardiac frequency components, and five EEG frequency bands. Global-average and spatial cluster-based permutation analyses were performed, with family-wise error rate correction across all 40 predefined BHI features. Results Compared with healthy controls, patients with schizophrenia showed higher theta, alpha, and beta EEG power during eyes-open rest and higher theta and alpha EEG power during eyes-closed rest after false discovery rate correction. Cardiac low-frequency (LF) and high-frequency (HF) spectral power did not differ significantly between groups. During eyes-open rest, patients showed lower global-average brain-to-heart high-frequency (BtH-HF) coupling across all five EEG bands (global family-wise error rate-corrected p = 0.0151-0.0349; Hedges' g = -0.911 to -0.841). This finding was supported by spatial cluster analysis and multitaper sensitivity analysis. No eyes-closed BtH-HF effects survived global correction. Although four eyes-open heart-to-brain (HtB) clusters were initially significant under the fixed-order model, none survived the Bayesian information criterion-based order sensitivity analysis. No significant Condition × Group interaction was detected across the five BtH-HF features. Conclusions Schizophrenia was associated with reduced eyes-open BtH-HF coupling across EEG bands, indicating altered statistical brain-heart coupling.

item.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

item.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

item.title: Bivariate Multiscale Sample Entropy of Frontoparietal–Subgenual ACC Dynamics in Depression During Accelerated TMS at 7 T
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective To examine whether longitudinal changes in frontoparietal (FP)–subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) joint temporal complexity differ between sgACC hemispheres in patients undergoing accelerated TMS (aTMS) and untreated healthy controls. Methods Twenty-four patients with current depressive episodes and fifteen healthy controls underwent 7T resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up. Patients received aTMS localized to the left DLPFC using Beam-F3. The same bilateral FP time series was paired separately with left and right sgACC time series. Bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) across scale factors a1–a10 was summarized by trapezoidal integration as a complexity index (bMSE-CI). The primary test was the Group × Time × sgACC Hemisphere interaction in a mixed repeated- measures ANOVA. Scale-specific interactions and clinical Spearman correlations were evaluated with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Change scores were follow-up minus baseline. Results The bMSE-CI Group × Time × Hemisphere interaction was significant (F(1,37) = 6.043, p = 0.0188, partial η² = 0.140). Mean left/right bMSE-CI changes were −0.286/+0.124 in patients and +0.323/+0.112 in controls. Of ten scale-specific three-way interactions, only a2 survived FDR correction (q = 0.0435). No baseline or change-score bMSE–MADRS association survived the specified FDR corrections. A random-intercept-only mixed-model sensitivity analysis did not reach statistical significance for the three-way interaction (p = 0.0718). Conclusion FP–sgACC joint temporal complexity showed hemisphere-dependent longitudinal differences between patients undergoing aTMS and healthy controls. These exploratory findings motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression. Independent replication, more precise reliability estimates, and prospective validation of clinical relevance are needed.

item.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

item.title: The Sv DC Field: Large-Scale and Hierarchical Functions Regulator.
item.description:
Research (Washington, D.C.)
Large-scale dynamic reorganization of brain functional networks has been extensively revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging, yet its direct electrophysiological basis remains unclear. In our prior research on epilepsy, we identified a distinctive electrophysiological phenomenon referred to as the slow-varying direct current (Sv DC, 0.01 to 0.5 Hz) field. This field demonstrates both the stability characteristic of a physical direct current and the slow-varying property of bioelectrical signals, enabling it to reflect the dynamic alterations in relative bioelectric field fluctuations. To further characterize its behavior across different functional states, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy patients implanted with depth electrodes during visual, motor, and language tasks. The Sv DC field exhibited large-scale convergence and suppression, accompanied by information transfer to other frequency bands, during these tasks. In visual functional areas, Sv DC field displayed rhythmic oscillations tightly coupled with gamma activity and increased power, whereas in nonvisual areas, Sv DC field power decreased significantly. During seizures, Sv DC field showed characteristic spatiotemporal spreading dynamics, a phenomenon consistently replicated in macaque monkeys, rats, and mice. These electrophysiological patterns suggest that the Sv DC field exhibits both large-scale cortical functional networks and region-specific modulations, potentially offering a novel understanding on dynamic organization of brain functional networks.

item.title: Denoised gray matter BOLD-CSF coupling in aging and its association with markers of preclinical AD
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Global gray matter (gGM) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal fluctuations are temporally coupled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflow. Reduced gGM BOLD-CSF coupling has been reported in aging and linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related pathology. Our study aimed to investigate the effect of multi-echo denoising on age-related reductions in coupling and whether coupling is associated with cortical thickness across AD-vulnerable regions and crystallized–fluid ability (‘CF’) discrepancy, markers of preclinical AD. We analyzed an open-access behavioral/MRI dataset (n = 301) cognitively healthy younger and older adults (OpenNeuro ds003592). Coupling scores were calculated as correlations between gGM signal fluctuations and CSF inflow signals, before and after denoising. Linear mixed models tested the effects of age and denoising on coupling, while multiple regression models assessed associations between denoised coupling, cortical thickness, and CFdiscrepancy. Coupling was lower in older versus younger adults. Denoising significantly reduced coupling in younger adults but not in older adults. Both gGM and CSF signal amplitudes were lower in older adults. Denoised coupling was not significantly associated with cortical thickness or CFdiscrepancy, and cortical thickness was not associated with CFdiscrepancy after controlling for age. These findings support age-related differences in BOLD–CSF coupling, which itself may not be related to coarse markers of preclinical AD.

item.title: Olfactory network variability is associated with odor identification and cognitive performance in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early marker of Alzheimer's disease pathology and predicts dementia conversion in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the pathophysiological role of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) variability within olfactory networks remains unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize seed-based dFC variability across olfactory pathways in MCI with odor identification impairment (MCI-OII) and examine its associations with olfactory and cognitive performance.MethodsNinety-seven patients with MCI were recruited and subdivided into MCI-OII and those without odor identification impairment (MCI-NOII), along with 97 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent neuropsychological assessment, olfactory testing, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Seed-based dFC variability was computed using a sliding window approach. Correlation and exploratory mediation analyses examined associations among abnormal dFC, odor identification, and cognition.ResultsCompared to MCI-NOII and HC, MCI-OII exhibited increased dFC variability between the left piriform cortex/right insula and right caudate nucleus, and between the left insula and left middle frontal gyrus. For the connection between the left insula and left cerebellar lobule VI, dFC variability showed a graded pattern from MCI-OII to HC to MCI-NOII. Increased caudate-centered dFC variability was associated with poorer odor identification, memory, and executive performance. Furthermore, exploratory mediation analyses suggested indirect associations involving odor identification, caudate-centered dFC variability, and memory or executive function.ConclusionsMCI-OII is characterized by increased olfactory-network dFC variability, particularly in caudate-centered pathways. These findings suggest that dFC variability may serve as a candidate network-level marker of concurrent olfactory impairment and cognitive dysfunction in MCI.

item.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced hemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid flow waves during sleep.
item.description:
Nature aging
Aging reduces the quality and quantity of sleep, and sleep disruption is predictive of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Sleep loss could affect brain health through disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, which is important for brain homeostasis. In young adults, large CSF flow waves appear during non-rapid eye movement sleep; however, whether sleep-dependent brain fluid physiology changes in aging is not known. Here we imaged large-scale CSF flow and hemodynamics in young (18-39 years) and older (60-84 years) adults during nighttime sleep. Sleep-dependent CSF flow was reduced in older adults, and was linked to reduced EEG slow wave power, decreased global hemodynamic oscillations and gray matter atrophy. Using sensory and vasoactive stimuli to drive CSF flow, we found that both neural and cerebrovascular changes contributed to this disruption. These results demonstrate reduced CSF flow during sleep in human aging, before disease onset, and identify parallel neural and hemodynamic mechanisms contributing to this decline.

item.title: Distinct cortical functional network alterations in internet gaming disorder and alcohol use disorder: A resting-state EEG graph theory analysis.
item.description:
Comprehensive psychiatry
Internet gaming disorder (IGD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are characterized by compulsive behaviors and impaired impulse control. Although IGD is classified as a behavioral addiction and AUD as a substance use disorder, previous studies have suggested potential neurophysiological similarities between the two conditions. However, the frequency-specific topological organization of cortical networks in IGD and AUD remains poorly understood. This study compared the cortical functional networks in IGD and AUD using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and graph theory-based network analysis. A total of 151 subjects (49 patients with IGD, 48 with AUD, and 54 healthy controls (HCs)) participated in this study. Resting-state EEG data were preprocessed, followed by source reconstruction and network analysis. We examined global and nodal network characteristics across different frequency bands. At the global network level, IGD exhibited a significantly higher clustering coefficient (CC) and strength (weighted degree) in the beta frequency band compared to AUD and HCs. At the nodal level, the IGD group displayed significantly increased beta-band CCs and strengths in multiple brain regions, particularly the parietal and limbic areas. Notably, beta-band nodal CC and strength in the bilateral superior frontal gyri were significantly lower in AUD than in IGD. Beta-band nodal CC and strength measures showed nominal associations with AUDIT or IAT scores. Our findings suggest that IGD and AUD exhibit distinct cortical network patterns. The results provide further neurophysiological evidence distinguishing IGD, as an example of behavioral addiction, from alcohol-related substance addiction.

item.title: Hemisphere-specific neuroplasticity after basal ganglia stroke: divergent patterns of brain reorganization revealed by fALFF and ReHo.
item.description:
Brain research
Background Lesion laterality modulates post-stroke neuroplasticity following basal ganglia infarction, but hemisphere-specific reorganization patterns of motor circuits remain unclear. Objective To investigate lateralized changes in spontaneous brain activity and local synchronization in patients with left versus right basal ganglia infarction using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), and to explore their associations with motor recovery. Methods Resting-state fMRI-derived fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were analyzed in 31 patients with left basal ganglia infarction (LBGIS), 33 patients with right basal ganglia infarction (RBGIS), and 33 healthy controls. TFCE-FWE corrected two-sample t-tests and covariate-adjusted partial correlations were used to compare brain activity and link functional alterations to Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) motor scores. Results LBGIS displayed hypoactivity in ipsilesional motor cortices alongside hyperactivation of contralesional cerebellum and prefrontal areas; ipsilesional sensorimotor ReHo positively correlated with FMA, whereas contralesional cerebellar fALFF negatively correlated with FMA. RBGIS showed reduced ipsilesional frontoparietal activity and isolated hyper-synchronization within the ipsilesional frontoparietal motor network without cerebellar recruitment, with elevated ReHo in ipsilesional precentral gyrus/SMA negatively associated with FMA. Direct group comparisons validated stronger bilateral motor-planning and contralesional cerebellar signals in LBGIS, and higher right visual-spatial fALFF in RBGIS. Conclusions Left and right basal ganglia infarctions elicit divergent hemispheric neuroplastic modifications in motor networks. These lateralized functional signatures could serve as imaging biomarkers for lesion-side-customized motor rehabilitation.

item.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

item.title: The extended default mode network dysconnectivity in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The default mode network (DMN) extends beyond cortex into subcortical structures, yet how this extended DMN (eDMN) is causally reorganized in schizophrenia (SZ) remains unclear. Here, resting-state fMRI from 74 healthy controls (HC) and 66 SZ patients was analyzed. Subject-specific eDMNs were identified using spatially-constrained independent component analysis, and effective connectivity among 13 regions was estimated with spectral dynamic causal modeling, with group effects assessed using parametric empirical Bayes. Causal centrality—a dynamics-sensitive and causality-based measure of nodal importance—was computed per region, compared between groups, and correlated with MATRICS cognitive scores in patients. Causal centrality rankings were highly similar across groups (ρ = 0.87), with both favoring subcortical over cortical regions. Group differences were regionally specific: temporal cortex was more causally central in patients, whereas posterior parietal cortex was more causally central in controls. Most connection-level SZ−HC differences originated from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, prefrontal cortex, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and thalamus. In patients, temporal causal centrality correlated negatively with reasoning/problem-solving, and ventrolateral prefrontal causal centrality with processing speed and composite cognition. The eDMN’s core causal architecture is preserved in schizophrenia, but temporal influence is enhanced and parietal influence attenuated— alterations that are behaviorally meaningful and consistent with pathological reorganization.

item.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure–Coupled and Structure–Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimer’s Disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R 2 = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimer’s disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.

item.title: Allometric scaling of resting-state EEG network topography across childhood and adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Brain network topography undergoes complex reorganization throughout childhood and adolescence. Quantifying the functional form of this maturation remains a key challenge. Here, we applied developmental allometry to sensor-level resting-state EEG networks from 1,957 participants aged 5–21 years (Healthy Brain Network). We fitted power laws of age to four graph-theoretic indices (small-worldness, global and local efficiency, modularity) across five frequency bands. Nineteen of the 20 band-by-index exponents were negative. Low-frequency (delta and theta) small-worldness showed the steepest declines (alpha = -0.878 and − 0.868), indicating a near-halving of the metric with each doubling of age. Lobe-resolved analyses revealed a pan-lobar but non-uniform decline, with posterior regions showing steeper age-related changes than frontal regions in specific bands. While raw-space cross-validation did not uniquely favor the power law over linear models, its scale-free exponent provides a unified parameter to compare developmental rates across spatial and spectral scales. Individual deviations from this topology did not track dimensional psychopathology. These exponents provide a quantitative reference for EEG network topography maturation and highlight the necessity of frequency- and region-specific modeling.

item.title: A realistic model of resting-state BOLD spectra in white matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state BOLD signals in white matter show a spectral elevation near 0.06 Hz on an exponentially decaying background, and white-matter hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) have a prominent initial dip. We model the resting signal as shot noise: randomly timed neural events are filtered by the HRF, so that the spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the squared HRF gain, plus instrumental noise. The initial dip and post-stimulus undershoot remove low-frequency power, making the white-matter HRF a band-pass filter with maximum gain near 0.05 Hz. One set of physiological parameters fits both a measured white-matter HRF (R² = 0.993) and the group-mean white-matter spectrum (R² = 0.987), with a resting transit time of about 4 s and a metabolic response weighted about twice as heavily as in gray matter. Deepening the dip raises the filter gain and moves its maximum toward 0.06 Hz, linking the dip to the spectral feature. A narrower line in individual spectra is reproduced either by an underdamped HRF that matches the measured response over its first 20 s or by a rhythmic input near 0.06 Hz. The model identifies which HRF properties could explain the decline of the peak with age.

item.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

item.title: Dynamic Brain Network Transitions and Sensorimotor Performance Across the Adult Lifespan.
item.description:
Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR
Background & objectives Healthy adult aging is accompanied by subtle variations in fine sensorimotor control and cognitive flexibility. Traditional static neuroimaging approaches often overlook short-term temporal dynamics. This study investigated cross-sectional associations between temporal brain state transitions and sensorimotor performance-specifically force matching and motor learning adaptation-across the adult lifespan. Methods Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and behavioral data from 218 healthy adults (aged 18-88 years; 99 females, 119 males) were analyzed across three age groups: young (18-35 years; n = 45; 25 females, 20 males), middle-aged (>35-60 years; n = 88; 37 females, 51 males), and older adults (>60 years; n = 85; 37 females, 48 males).Sex distribution did not differ significantly across age groups (p = 0.302). Time varying functional connectivity was modeled to extract Fractional Occupancy (FO), Mean Dwell Time (MDT), and global Switching Rate (SR) across six recurrent brain states. Behavioral metrics included finger force overcompensation (force matching) and spatial trajectory error during late-exposure motor learning. Results Advancing age was significantly associated with higher trajectory error during motor learning (p < 0.001) and greater force overcompensation (p ≤ 0.001). Post-hoc comparisons revealed non-linear cross-sectional differences, with older adults exhibiting higher error margins than young and middle-aged groups. Global switching rate (SR) demonstrated a statistically significant inverse association with motor learning error (β = -0.122 to -0.280, p < 0.03), indicating that higher dynamic network flexibility is associated with lower motor adaptation error. Furthermore, age was negatively correlated with switching rate (β = -0.166, p = 0.023). In the Executive Control Network (State 3), females exhibited significantly higher FO (p = 0.003) and adjusted MDT (p = 0.007) compared to males. Additionally, older males showed a nominal positive association with Task-Positive Network (State 5) dwell time (ρ = 0.204, p = 0.026). Conclusion These findings suggest an age-associated pattern of "dynamic rigidity," characterized by a reduced propensity for global brain state switching within cross-sectional observations. Fluid state transition capacity-rather than isolated state occupancy-offers significant explanatory relevance for sensorimotor adaptation across the adult lifespan.

item.title: Brain mediation network reveals aberrant multivariate interactions in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Journal of psychiatric research
The brain is a complex and highly interconnected network system consisting of numerous regions. Previous studies have revealed disruptions in pairwise interactions between brain regions of schizophrenia (SCZ). However, the alterations of multivariate interactions at the whole-cortex scale in SCZ remain unclear. The subjects comprised 42 SCZ patients and 50 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. We employed our recently proposed Independent Component Mediation Network (ICMN) to investigate how the interaction between any two brain regions in SCZ is modulated by a third region, and further introduced mediation ability (MA) and mediated strength (MS) metrics. MA measures how effectively a node serves as a mediator for information communication between any other pair of brain regions. MS quantifies the extent to which a node's information exchange with other nodes depends on indirect pathways via a mediator. Our results revealed decreased MS in the visual, somatomotor, dorsal attention, ventral attention, and frontoparietal networks in SCZ patients, whereas MA remained preserved in these networks. The limbic network showed a dual reduction in both MA and MS, and the dorsal attention network also exhibited a lack of high-intensity MS. Additionally, we found that MA predicted positive symptoms, whereas MS predicted overall psychopathology in SCZ patients. The MS was generally reduced in SCZ patients, revealing a widespread decline in indirect interaction strength. Furthermore, our mediation metrics could effectively predict clinical symptoms. This may not only deepen the understanding of neuropathology from a network perspective but also facilitate more targeted and effective treatments for SCZ.

item.title: High cortical lesion burden moderates the association between brain networks and processing speed in older adults with multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Cortical lesions (CL) are common in older adults with multiple sclerosis (OAMS), but their influence on the relationship between resting-state network strength (RSNS) and cognitive function in OAMS remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether CL moderates associations between RSNS and processing speed in OAMS. 82 OAMS participants (mean age: 64.4 ± 4.1 years; males/females: 26/56) were scanned in a 3T scanner. Identification of CL on double inversion-recovery (DIR) MRI images in this study was performed using established consensus recommendations. We estimated functional brain networks using a data-driven procedure to extract seven intrinsic resting-state networks. The Symbol-Digit-Modalities Test (SDMT), an established test of processing speed and working memory, served as the cognitive outcome measure. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, examined the relationship between RSNS and SDMT performance with CL (three levels: no CL, 1-2 CL, and ≥ 3 CL) as a moderator. Significant CL-by-network interactions in models adjusted for sociodemographic covariates and white matter lesion load indicated that high-burden CL vs. no CL moderated the association between RSNS and SDMT in the auditory network (AUD) (p = 0.030), dorsal attention network (DAN) (p = 0.033), left frontoparietal network (LFPN) (p = 0.030), and posterior DMN (pDMN) (p = 0.030). Conditional effects showed that high-burden CLs attenuated positive associations between specific brain networks and SDMT performance. These findings suggest that higher CL burden restricts the functional brain support for processing speed and working memory performance in OAMS.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.
